Considering the hype surrounding No Man's Sky, I thought this postmortem of SPORE would be interesting to read.

I would say the comparison would be more apt to a current in-development title like Star Citizen, which is mirroring a lot of the "multiple genre" concerns that came up with Spore. I feel like the main issue with Spore is that they effectively were building 4-5 separate game titles and trying to mash them together into a single experience. I'm not getting that same feeling from No Man's Sky.

No Man's Sky is more a problem of content generation. Is whatever mechanism they use to generate worlds capable of generating worlds that people actually want to play in? Technically, they could solve the problem by just throwing money at the problem and having developers/designers build or enhance worlds manually and go from there.

With the amount of content they want generated, it couldn't be designed manually. Spore had other problems too. Including a higher up dumbing the game down significantly. It's a good example of executive meddling.

It's a good example of executive meddling.

It is not. As Soren Johnson's postmortem explains, Spore's biggest problems stemmed from internal disagreements among the developers, incohesive design leading to mechanics that undermined the game's theme, and the sheer scale of the game.

Don't get me wrong it's not the only problem the game had, but there was definitely some executive meddling involved. Can't remember who, but someone made them slap googly eyes on everything and simplify the mechanics.

Like I said, if you read the postmortem which was written by one of the developers of Spore, the cute pressure came primarily from within the team, and from the lack of a unified design direction.

Unfortunately, the Spore team was chronically fractured, divided into factions which had completely different priorities for the project. One well-known divide was the cute-vs-science debate; the ‘cute’ team wanted a playful, emotionally engaging experience while the ‘science’ team wanted an accurate representation of how the universe worked. I joined the team after a tenuous compromise was struck, which attempted to combine cute mechanics with a scientific theme.

However, I witnessed a new divide among the team which was less well-known; ... a cultural gap emerged between the newer ‘gameplay’ team and the older ‘Sim’ team. The former group ... was primarily concerned with how Spore played as a game. ... Did the player’s choices matter? ... In contrast, the ‘Sim’ ... was more comfortable with Spore as a toy box. Could the players express themselves? Was sharing one’s creations with other players meaningful? Did the game spark the imagination?

These cultural divides ruined Spore’s chances to be a focused, cohesive experience. Spore could have worked either as a cute game or as a scientific one. It could have been a series of interesting decisions or the best set of magic crayons ever devised.

And here's what Will Wright, one of the people leading the "science" faction, had to say about Spore's development.

I see that many of the criticisms about the depth of play in Spore seem to be personally directed to Chris Hecker in particular. This is both ironic and incorrect...

To take a quick tangent let me use the creature design vs. performance as an example. We had competing issues to face. First, we wanted the creature’s design to impact its in-game performance. Second, we wanted the economics of the editor to be simple and understandable and connected to performance. Third, we wanted a high amount of aesthetic diversity. We didn’t want there to be one ultimate design direction that the simulator was forcing all the creatures into. In other words if to be fast you had to have long legs that would have met the first goal, conflicted with the third goal and made the second much more complex.
I should get around to reading the full postmortem some time. I hope someone manages to pull the design off some day.

I wish you'd read Soren Johnson's postmortem before making assumptions about my taste in games and my expectations of No Man's Sky. Johnson's postmortem outlines the major obstacles faced by Spore's developers, obstacles that face many games, especially those of similar scope or concepts. Sharing a link to that postmortem is not equivalent to a tirade against No Man's Sky. You're arguing against a stance that was never made in this thread or its linked content.

Johnson's first point was about Spore's two biggest concepts: "powers of ten and procedural content".

Spore’s biggest issue was that the play at each stage was fairly shallow because the team was making five games at once. ... Some effort was made, of course, to share ideas and elements across stages; however, the compromises involved often watered down what was supposed to make each stage distinct in the first place. ... Thus, the powers of ten idea put the team in a state of perpetual compromise where every major decision had to be considered according to its effect across all five stages.

On the other hand, procedural content was a genuinely interesting and fertile idea – one which was novel for the time, appropriate for a game about evolution, and rich with gameplay possibilities. The tragedy of Spore is that the team never re-evaluated its first big idea in comparison to its second one.

No Man's Sky also seems to be focusing on two big concepts. The one that I think excites most people (including myself) is the exploration of a procedurally generated universe. But on top of that, the developers are tasked with simulating a living economy with competing parties.

Sean Murray: We want trading to be fun, we want it to be understandable because already the game's quite large. We are trying to simulate a universe that has trade, traders, pirates, and different factions. ... [If] you just don't like visiting planets, you want to play a space game, you can do that if you want.

Murray has acknowledged that he doesn't understand the choice to play as a trader because eventually, a monotonous routine sets in and it becomes "the closest thing you can do to a boring job" and so is a choice that he doesn't understand. When a game "is all about exploration" it is not a stretch to wonder if these trading mechanics undermines its theme and if the resources expended on those aspects of would be better directed somewhere else. That is the second obstacle to Spore's development in Johnson's postmortem.

The third obstacle detailed by Johnson was the sheer scale of Spore, which made it difficult to see early on whether the game as a whole was cohesive and enjoyable. No Man's Sky isn't even out yet and there isn't enough information available about how the development itself is going, but Johnson's words on the subject are true and I think should be kept in mind by all developers.

... fully playable "prototypes" signal the beginning of the most crucial part of game development – when the designers can change the game rapidly based on feedback from actual playthroughs, not disparate, standalone experiments. A game must be greater than the sum of its parts, and the gameplay systems can only be understood when they exist within one complete experience ... Spore was not fully playable until, at best, the final year of the project. ... Of course, many successful games are not fully playable until months before release, but they tend to be part of established genres or franchises; the fun was already found in previous versions, and the team simply needs to improve the core gameplay without ruining anything.

The fourth and last obstacle in Johnson's postmortem of Spore is the lack of cohesion among the developers. There was no shortage of talent, but there were incompatible and conflicting design goals that could not be reconciled. It's true that no one outside of the No Man Sky's development team can make unequivocal statements on whether this is an obstacle they face, but it's important to remember nonetheless.

Unfortunately, the Spore team was chronically fractured, divided into factions which had completely different priorities for the project. ... [A] tenuous compromise was struck, which attempted to combine cute mechanics with a scientific theme. ... These cultural divides ruined Spore’s chances to be a focused, cohesive experience.
